new = """      # tmux gives tests/tui.sh the pty that curses needs. Without it
      # that test reports SKIPPED and the job still goes green, so the
      # only coverage of the full-screen display would quietly be none.
      #
      # Bounded and retried, because an unguarded install can take the
      # whole job with it. Measured on #185: apt-get update hung on
      # ubuntu-latest and the job's 15 minutes ran out inside this step,
      # three attempts running -- Configure, Build and Test all skipped,
      # nothing compiled, and the check reporting `cancelled`, which is
      # also what GitHub says when a human presses the button or when
      # the concurrency group above fires. It took a per-step API query
      # to find out the runner had simply failed to install tmux.
      #
      # timeout(1) is what does the work here, not the loop. A hang
      # never returns, so a retry alone never gets a second attempt:
      # measured, a three-pass loop around a hanging command makes
      # exactly one. Bounding each command turns the hang into an exit
      # status the loop can act on, and three tries at two minutes cost
      # at most six of the fifteen rather than all of them.
      #
      # timeout-minutes on the step as well, as a backstop for anything
      # that outlives its own bound -- and because a step that fails on
      # its own timeout keeps its log, where a job killed by the job
      # timeout does not.
      - name: Install ncurses and tmux
        if: runner.os == 'Linux'
        timeout-minutes: 8
        run: |
          for attempt in 1 2 3; do
            if timeout 120 sudo apt-get update &&
               timeout 180 sudo apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \\
                 libncurses-dev tmux; then
              exit 0
            fi
            echo "::warning::apt attempt $attempt failed or timed out" >&2
            sleep 10
          done
          echo "::error::could not install libncurses-dev and tmux" >&2
          exit 1

      - name: Install tmux
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        timeout-minutes: 8
        env:
          HOMEBREW_NO_AUTO_UPDATE: 1
        run: |
          brew list tmux >/dev/null 2>&1 && exit 0
          for attempt in 1 2 3; do
            if timeout 300 brew install tmux; then
              exit 0
            fi
            echo "::warning::brew attempt $attempt failed or timed out" >&2
            sleep 10
          done
          echo "::error::could not install tmux" >&2
          exit 1
"""

open(p, "wb").write(data.replace(old, new).encode("utf-8"))
print("ok")

input.prompt:
Read .claude/agents/verifier.md and follow it. Verify the working tree of /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek on branch ci/guard-dependency-install. All changes are uncommitted; `git diff main` is the whole change — one file, `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

**What the change does (issue #186).** The job sets `timeout-minutes: 15` and installed dependencies with an unguarded `sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install ...`. When apt hung on `ubuntu-latest` — which it did on PR #185, three attempts running — it consumed the entire job budget. GitHub killed the job, `Configure`/`Build`/`Test` were all skipped, nothing compiled, and the check reported `cancelled`, which is also what GitHub says when a human presses the button or when the workflow's own `concurrency: cancel-in-progress` fires. Logs are not retained for a step killed by the job timeout, so there was nothing to read; it took a per-step API query to establish that the runner had simply failed to install tmux.

The change bounds each install command with `timeout(1)`, wraps them in a three-attempt loop, and adds `timeout-minutes: 8` to both install steps (Linux apt and macOS brew) as a backstop. The key point, which is in the comment: `timeout(1)` is what does the work, not the loop — a hang never returns, so a retry alone never gets a second attempt.

**What I have already checked myself**, and would like you to confirm independently rather than repeat blindly:
- The YAML parses and both install steps carry `timeout-minutes: 8` while the job keeps 15.
- Both `run:` bodies pass `bash -n` and `shellcheck -s bash` when extracted from the YAML.
- I exercised both bodies end to end against stand-in `apt-get`/`brew`/`sudo` binaries on `PATH` with the timeouts shortened: a permanent hang fails cleanly with a readable `::error::` after three bounded attempts; a *transient* hang (first call hangs, second succeeds) recovers with rc=0, which is the actual observed pattern — `ubuntu-latest ci-debug` hung once on #185 and passed on rerun; a healthy install passes first time; and on macOS the `brew list tmux` fast path exits 0 without touching brew.
- Separately, I demonstrated the counterfactual: a three-pass retry loop with no `timeout` makes exactly one attempt against a hanging command.

**Scope is yours to decide** and I am not going to tell you it is small. Nothing compiled changes — same presets, same flags, same commands in `Configure`/`Build`/`Test` — so I would not expect the game's behaviour to move, but that is a claim worth checking rather than asserting, and the whole point of the change is that CI is the thing that verifies CI. In particular I would value your judgement on whether the bounds are right: 120s for `apt-get update`, 180s for `apt-get install`, 300s for `brew install`, three attempts each, 10s between, against a 15-minute job in which `ctest` alone takes about six minutes per configuration on this machine. If a worst case of three failed attempts plus the suite could still exceed 15 minutes, say so.

Report failures, flakes, missing coverage and environment issues. Read-only: report findings, never fix them.

#168 is merged and I've moved on to **#186**, the CI fragility that cost four attempts to merge it.

The fix bounds each dependency-install command with `timeout(1)` inside a three-attempt loop, plus a step-level `timeout-minutes: 8` on both installers. The insight worth stating: **the retry isn't what fixes this — the timeout is.** A hang never returns, so a retry loop alone gets exactly one attempt; I demonstrated that before writing the change. Bounding each command turns the hang into an exit status the loop can act on.

I exercised both step bodies end to end against stand-in `apt-get`/`brew` binaries: a permanent hang fails in ~6 seconds with a readable `::error::`, a *transient* hang recovers with rc=0 — which is the pattern actually observed, since `ci-debug` hung once and passed on rerun — and the healthy path is untouched.

I've asked the verifier to check one thing I can't settle alone: whether three failed attempts plus a ~6-minute `ctest` can still exceed the 15-minute job budget. If they can, the bounds are wrong.

`ui-review` won't bind here — nothing compiled changes, same presets and flags — but I'll state that explicitly to `code-review` and in the commit rather than let it pass silently.

One deterministic, blocking defect, plus a comment whose arithmetic does not hold. Everything that compiles and runs is green.

---

## Failures

### 1. Blocking — the macOS step depends on `timeout(1)`, which GitHub macOS runners do not have

`/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/.github/workflows/ci.yml:81` now runs `timeout 300 brew install tmux`. `timeout(1)` is GNU coreutils; macOS ships BSD userland and does not have it. Both macOS legs (`ci-debug`, `ci-release`) fail deterministically at the install step, roughly 30 seconds in, and `Configure`/`Build`/`Test` are skipped.

This repository already says so, twice, in its own words:

- `/home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek/CMakeLists.txt:65-66` — "TIMEOUT because the script's own `timeout` guard needs coreutils, which macOS runners do not have."
- commit `ec60e78` — "a CTest TIMEOUT, since the script's `timeout` guard needs coreutils that macOS runners lack."
- and five test scripts guard it: `tests/journey.sh:60`, `tests/eof.sh:38`, `tests/help.sh:51`, `tests/golden.sh:82`, `tests/tournament.sh:109` all wrap it in `if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1`. The workflow does not.

Corroborated independently of the repo: `images/macos/toolsets/toolset-15.json` in `actions/runner-images` lists no `coreutils` in `common_packages`, and the macOS 14/15/26 image readmes never mention it (they name `gtar` for GNU tar, which is the same pattern).

The fast path does not save it — tmux is *not* preinstalled on the image. From this repo's own last green macOS job (`96288433362`, 2026-08-19), the old `brew list tmux || brew install tmux` line took the install branch:

```
2026-08-19T08:16:44.0354400Z ==> Would install 1 formula:
2026-08-19T08:16:44.0355000Z tmux
2026-08-19T08:16:45.8141090Z ==> Installing tmux
```

So `brew list tmux` fails and the new loop is entered every run. Reproduced locally by running the step body extracted from the YAML with a `PATH` that has a working `brew` stand-in but no `timeout`, which is exactly the runner's condition:

```
$ PATH=<stub> /bin/bash -e mac.sh
mac.sh: line 3: timeout: command not found
::warning::brew attempt 1 failed or timed out      (x3)
::error::could not install tmux
rc=1 after 30s
```

With `timeout` on `PATH` the same body is `rc=0` in 0s. Deterministic, three for three.

Worth noting how this reads against issue #186, which records "both macOS legs passed every time, having no apt step": the change breaks the two legs that were never affected by the bug it fixes. The Linux half of the change is sound — I reproduced healthy (rc=0, 1s), permanent hang (rc=1 after three bounded attempts), and transient hang (rc=0 on attempt 2) against stand-in `sudo`/`apt-get` with the bounds shortened, matching what you reported.

### 2. The comment's budget arithmetic is wrong, in a comment AGENTS.md reads as specification

`ci.yml:50-51`: "three tries at two minutes cost at most six of the fifteen rather than all of them."

A try is two bounded commands, not one: `timeout 120` plus `timeout 180` is 300s. The `sleep 10` also runs after the third failed attempt, since it is inside the loop body. Worst case inside the step is `3 x (120 + 180) + 3 x 10 = 930s = 15m30s` — more than the whole job budget, not six minutes of it. Confirmed by the shortened-bounds run: with 3/4/1 substituted, the permanent-hang case took exactly 12s = `3 x (3 + 4 - 3... )`, i.e. `3 x (3 + 1)` with the install short-circuited, and three sleeps.

What actually caps it is the step's own `timeout-minutes: 8` (480s), so the true statement is "at most eight of the fifteen". Two consequences the comment does not mention:

- **The three-attempt design is not reachable in the worst case.** If `apt-get install` is the hanging command rather than `apt-get update`, an attempt costs `t_update + 180 + 10` ≈ 210s, so attempt 3 starts at ~420s and is cut off, or never starts at all if attempts run to their full 300s (attempt 3 would begin at 620s > 480s). For the mode actually observed on #185 — `update` hangs, `install` short-circuited by `&&` — an attempt costs 130s and all three fit in 390s, so the fix does cover the bug it was written for.
- **The bounds are advisory, not enforced,** because `timeout` is used without `-k`. Measured locally against a child that traps `TERM`: `timeout 3` returned rc=124 but only after 30s of wall clock; `timeout -k 1 3` returned rc=137 after 4s. A wedged apt (or one in uninterruptible D-state on a stuck mirror, which is the shape of the #185 hang) is precisely the case where SIGTERM may not land. The 8-minute step cap is what really bounds this, which is an argument for the backstop, not against it — but it makes "at most six" doubly unsupported.

---

## On the bounds, since you asked

Measured, from this repo's CI and this machine:

| | Install | Test | Job total |
|---|---|---|---|
| ubuntu ci-debug (job 96288415812) | 35s | 5m32s | 6m12s |
| ubuntu ci-release (job 96288415250) | 6s | 5m25s | 5m36s |
| macOS ci-debug (job 96288433362) | 4s | 5m53s | 6m09s |
| local `ctest --preset ci-debug` | — | 379.8s | — |
| local `ctest --preset ci-release` | — | 370.7s | — |

Non-install overhead is ~5m40s, so the slack against the 15-minute job budget is ~9m20s.

- **Three *failed* attempts cannot exceed 15 minutes.** The step cap fires at 8 minutes and the job then fails, with the step's log retained. That is the outcome the change is for, and it works.
- **The case that can still hit the job wall is a *successful* install that runs near the cap.** 8 minutes of install plus ~6 minutes of suite is ~14 minutes against a 15-minute job — about a minute of slack, and #101 records `tui` growing (it was 195s of the 380s local run). That is the same failure mode the change exists to remove: job killed, logs lost, check reads `cancelled`. Issue #186 asked for "two or three minutes" on the step so "the remaining time still runs the tests"; 8 minutes is nearly the whole slack budget. A cap of ~4 minutes, or per-command bounds of 60/120 (3 attempts, ~6 min ceiling), would keep the three attempts and the arithmetic consistent with each other.

One further limitation, reasoned rather than measured: a `timeout`-killed `apt-get install` can leave dpkg mid-transaction, and the retry will then hit "dpkg was interrupted, you must manually run `dpkg --configure -a`". The retry is effective against an `update` hang (the observed mode) and likely not against an `install` hang.

Not a finding: `::warning::`/`::error::` written to stderr is parsed by the runner. Evidence in the same job log — Homebrew's own `opoo` output, which goes to stderr, was rendered as `##[warning]The following taps are not trusted:`.

---

## Problem

Nothing in the repository checks `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. There is no
`actionlint`, no YAML lint, and no shellcheck over the `run:` bodies —
which are shell scripts that no local pass ever sees. The macOS branch
in particular is exercised only by a macOS runner.

## Why it matters

It is not hypothetical. On the branch for #186 I wrote an install step
that called `timeout 300 brew install tmux`. `timeout(1)` is GNU
coreutils and the GitHub macOS runners do not ship it, so both macOS
legs would have failed deterministically at that step — the two legs the
bug being fixed had never touched.

This repository already knew that fact and wrote it down twice:

- `CMakeLists.txt:64-65` — "TIMEOUT because the script's own `timeout`
  guard needs coreutils, which macOS runners do not have."
- and five scripts guard it: `tests/journey.sh:60`, `tests/eof.sh:38`,
  `tests/help.sh:51`, `tests/golden.sh:82`, `tests/tournament.sh:109`
  all wrap it in `if command -v timeout >/dev/null 2>&1`.

So the knowledge was in the tree, in the idiom, in a comment — and none
of it was reachable by any check that runs before CI. The defect was
caught by the `verifier` reading the workflow against `CMakeLists.txt`,
which is a person noticing, not a mechanism.

The general shape: a `run:` body is the one kind of code in this
repository that is written in a language we lint everywhere else and
never lint here.

## Relation to #106

#106 asks for shellcheck over `tests/*.sh`. This is the same argument
one directory over, and the workflow bodies are arguably worse off: a
test script at least runs on every `ctest`, where a `run:` body's
non-Linux branch runs only on a runner nobody can reproduce locally.
Whoever takes #106 should probably take this at the same time — the
mechanism is the same, and `actionlint` bundles shellcheck for exactly
this purpose.

## Fixing it

- `actionlint` in CI and/or as a `ctest` case. It parses the workflow
  schema *and* runs shellcheck over each `run:` body, which is both
  halves of this.
- Failing that, a small test that extracts every `run:` body with a YAML
  parser and pipes it through `sh -n` and `shellcheck`. That is what I
  did by hand on the #186 branch; it is worth not being by hand.
- Neither catches "this binary is absent on that runner image", which is
  the actual defect above. A lint rule for it would be bespoke; what
  would catch it is a `command -v` guard being the house idiom, which it
  already is in `tests/` — so a grep-level check that a workflow calling
  `timeout` also guards it is cheap and would have fired here.

## Where it was found

By the `verifier` on the branch for #186, which reported the defect as
blocking and noted that nothing in the repository would have caught it.
Filed separately because the fix is a new check, which is not what #186
is about.
EOF

**F3 — "an attempt is at most 60 + 120 = 180s" is not an upper bound.** With `-k 10` on each `bound`, a TERM-ignoring child adds up to 10s per command: 70+130 = 200s. The comment invokes exactly that child two paragraphs earlier as the reason for `-k`.

**F4 — "an attempt costs 65s and all three fit in 205s".** At 65s per iteration, three is 195s; 205 does not derive from the stated figures.

None of these changes behavior — the conclusion "more than the cap, which truncates it" survives all four.

**F5 (evidence for a resolution you already recorded, slightly understated).** Your dpkg resolution is right and I am not disputing it, but the measurement is sharper than "can leave dpkg mid-transaction": when the root child ignores TERM, `-k` kills the *sudo front end* and the root child survives orphaned and keeps running —

```
survivors after timeout returned:   197  0  sleep 31
survivors 4s later:                 197  0  sleep 31
```

**7 minutes is right; I endorse it.** Measured here: ctest 378s / 368s, clean build 3s, configure ~1s. gh issue create --title "AGENTS.md says a full ctest is about four minutes per configuration; it is over six" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`AGENTS.md:425`, in the "Who runs which tests" section, says:

> Running the suite twice buys nothing and costs the whole of it: a full
> `ctest` here is about four minutes per configuration.

Measured repeatedly on this machine over the last two branches:

| run | configuration | wall |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ctest --preset ci-debug` | Debug | 377.8s / 378.4s / 379.8s |
| `ctest --preset ci-release` | Release | 368.3s / 368.7s / 370.7s |

That is **6m10s and 6m10s**, not four minutes — out by about 55%.

## Why it matters

The sentence is doing work, not decoration. It is the cost argument for
the whole main-agent/`verifier` split: it is why the main agent is told
not to pre-run the battery, and why a second full run is called a waste.
The argument gets *stronger* with the true number, so nothing built on
it is wrong — but the figure is the one a reader will quote when
deciding whether some new pass is affordable, and it is now the third
stale timing claim found in this repository, after `CMakeLists.txt`'s
"~11s" for the `tui` test (#101) and my own bad estimate in #101's
comments.

It also interacts with two open issues:

- **#101** — `tui` alone is 195s of that ~378s, and growing.
- **#186** — the CI job budget is 15 minutes, so a ~6-minute suite per
  configuration leaves much less slack for anything before it than a
  4-minute one implies. That is the arithmetic the install-step cap in
  #186 had to be sized against.

## Where it was found

By `code-review` on the branch for #186, which noticed the workflow
comment citing "about six minutes per configuration" and flagged that it
contradicted `AGENTS.md:425` — one of the two written numbers had to be
stale, and it is this one. Filed rather than fixed on that branch, per
step 9: the branch is a CI workflow change and `AGENTS.md` is not in its
diff.

## Fixing it

Replace the figure, and consider whether it should be a figure at all.
Three of these have now gone stale. Something like "a full `ctest` here
runs for minutes per configuration, most of it the `tui` test" carries
the argument without a number that has to be maintained — and where a
number is genuinely wanted, saying where and when it was measured is
what the repository asks of comments elsewhere.

git add -A && git commit -F - <<'EOF'
ci: bound and retry the dependency install

An unguarded install can take the whole job with it. Measured on #185:
apt-get update hung on ubuntu-latest and the job's 15 minutes ran out
inside that step -- 911s of a 916s job -- across three job re-runs.
Configure, Build and Test were skipped every time, nothing compiled,
and the check reported `cancelled`, which is also what GitHub says when
a human presses the button or when this workflow's own concurrency
group fires. Logs are not retained for a step killed by the job
timeout, so it took a per-step API query to establish that the runner
had simply failed to install tmux.

timeout(1) is what fixes this, not the retry. A hang never returns, so
a loop alone never gets a second attempt: measured, a three-pass loop
around a hanging command makes exactly one. Bounding each command turns
the hang into a status the loop can act on.

timeout goes inside sudo so that it runs as root with apt-get as its
direct child. Outside, it is an unprivileged process signalling a root
one: the kill fails, the front end dies at the bound, and the root
apt-get survives orphaned holding the apt lock, so the next attempt
fails on the lock rather than retrying the fetch. Measured both ways in
a container against an unroutable mirror; inside sudo, nothing survives.

The loop names the command that failed and reads its status -- 124 the
bound, 137 the -k after it, anything else apt's own -- because #186's
complaint was that a red log did not say what had gone wrong. Written
as `cmd || rc=$?` rather than an if around the command: $? after a
closed if is the statement's status, so a first draft reported every
install failure as "status 0", and a bare failing command would trip
the errexit the runner's default `bash -e {0}` turns on.

Both steps carry timeout-minutes: 7. It backstops anything outliving
its own bound, and a step that fails on its own timeout keeps its log
where a job killed by the job timeout does not. 7 rather than 8 because
the two budgets add only on success -- a failed install skips the rest
of the job -- so an install that succeeds slowly must still leave room
for ctest, which the runners put at 333s and 325s for the two presets.

The macOS step calls no timeout at all: it is GNU coreutils and those
runners do not have it. This repository already knew that, in
CMakeLists.txt and in five scripts under tests/ that guard the call
with command -v, and a first draft of this change called it unguarded
there -- which would have failed both macOS legs deterministically, the
two the bug never touched. The verifier caught it.

ui-review did not run: nothing compiled changes. Same presets, same
flags, and Configure, Build and Test are byte-identical, so that pass
has no screen to read. code-review agreed the skip three times.

the portability defect above reached review unchallenged) and #188
(AGENTS.md puts a full ctest at four minutes per configuration;
measured it is over six).

Closes #186
